subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Cost of Extreme Weather
description: A quick, practical guide to The Cost of Extreme Weather.

hook.text: In 2023, the world experienced 28 weather disasters that each caused over $1 billion in damage.

buildup.text: The economic cost of extreme weather has grown fivefold since the 1980s.

discovery.text: Part of this is more people and wealth in harm's way. But the weather itself is getting worse.

twist.text: Insurance companies are retreating from high-risk areas, leaving millions without coverage.

climax.text: Developing nations suffer the greatest losses relative to their economies — and have the least insurance.

punchline.text: Extreme weather has a price tag. And the bill is growing every year.

quiz.question: How has the economic cost of extreme weather changed since the 1980s?

details.summary: Global economic losses from extreme weather disasters have more than doubled since the 1990s, exceeding 300 billion dollars in several recent years. Climate change, urbanization, and growing wealth exposure are all driving costs higher.
details.whyItMatters: Rising disaster costs strain insurance systems, government budgets, and economic development. Understanding these trends shapes debates over who should pay for climate impacts.
takeaways: Weather disaster costs have roughly doubled since the 1990s
Most losses are uninsured, especially in developing countries
A single major hurricane can cost over 100 billion dollars

faq.question: How much of the cost increase is due to climate change versus development?
faq.answer: Both factors contribute. More people and property in vulnerable areas increase exposure, while climate change increases event frequency and intensity. Studies suggest climate change is responsible for roughly 30 to 50 percent of the cost increase.

faq.question: Can insurance absorb rising extreme weather costs?
faq.answer: Insurance is retreating from high-risk areas as losses mount. Insurers have withdrawn from parts of Florida and California, and many developing nations have almost no weather insurance. The protection gap between losses and coverage is widening.
